figures.description: Background General introduction to micropile technology for transportation engineers evaluating deep foundation alternatives. Micropiles are small-diameter (100-300 mm) drilled and grouted replacement piles Originated in Italy in the 1950s as 'pali radice' (root piles) by Dr. Fernando Lizzi Originally developed for underpinning historic structures damaged in World War II First used in the United States in the mid-1970s Significant growth in transportation applications since the early 1990s Can be installed in almost any ground type including access-restricted and low-headroom conditions Minimal noise and vibration during installation compared to driven piles

CASE 1: Directly loaded elements functioning as individual structural members or small groups CASE 1 applications: new foundations, underpinning, seismic retrofit, scour protection CASE 1 is the most common micropile application in the US CASE 2: Reticulated network reinforcing the soil mass as an in-situ composite CASE 2 applications: slope stabilization, earth retention, settlement reduction CASE 2 relies on micropile-soil interaction rather than individual element capacity CASE 2 is more common in European practice

figures.description: Classification by Method of Grouting Selection and specification of grouting method based on ground conditions and required bond capacity. Type A: Gravity grout only; lowest bond values; best in rock or very stiff cohesive soils Type B: Pressure grouting during casing withdrawal at 0.5-1.0 MPa; most common in US Type C: Gravity grout followed by one pressure injection at >1.0 MPa; French practice Type D: Gravity grout followed by multiple injections via tube-a-manchette at 2-8 MPa; highest bond Grouting method directly controls grout-to-ground bond capacity Bond strength increases from Type A through Type D Type B is the most common grouting method in US transportation practice

figures.description: Introduction and Design Overview Complete design framework for CASE 1 micropile structure foundation support. 12-step design process for CASE 1 micropiles (Table 5-1) 8 additional design considerations beyond the 12 primary steps Both structural (internal) and geotechnical (external) limit states must be checked Structural design ensures cross-section capacity for applied loads Geotechnical design ensures adequate grout-to-ground bond resistance Design covers compression, tension, lateral loading, combined stresses, and buckling Table 5-1 provides the complete design procedure framework

figures.description: Structural Design of Cased Length Structural design of the upper cased portion of micropiles for compression, tension, and combined loading. Three structural checks: compression (Eq. 5-1), tension (Eq. 5-2), combined stress (Eq. 5-3) Compression: P_c = 0.40*f'c*A_grout + 0.47*Fy*(A_bar + A_casing) Tension: P_t = 0.55*Fy*(A_bar + A_casing); no grout contribution Combined check: f_a/F_a + f_b/F_b <= 1.0 (interaction formula) Section properties: composite I, S, and r using modular ratios (Eq. 5-4a,b,c) Stress factors 0.40 (grout) and 0.47 (steel) from AASHTO Center bar provides additional capacity for both compression and tension

figures.description: Structural Design of Cased Length Structural design of the upper cased portion of micropiles for compression, tension, and combined loading. Three structural checks: compression (Eq. 5-1), tension (Eq. 5-2), combined stress (Eq. 5-3) Compression: P_c = 0.40*f'c*A_grout + 0.47*Fy*(A_bar + A_casing) Tension: P_t = 0.55*Fy*(A_bar + A_casing); no grout contribution Combined check: f_a/F_a + f_b/F_b <= 1.0 (interaction formula) Section properties: composite I, S, and r using modular ratios (Eq. 5-4a,b,c) Stress factors 0.40 (grout) and 0.47 (steel) from AASHTO Center bar provides additional capacity for both compression and tension

figures.caption: End-bearing Resistance of Piles in Layered Soils
figures.description: Structural Design of Uncased Length Structural design of the uncased bond zone for micropiles with center reinforcing bar only. Uncased length is the bond zone where load transfers through grout-to-ground bond Compression (Eq. 5-7): P_c = 0.40*f'c*A_grout + 0.47*Fy*A_bar (no casing term) Tension (Eq. 5-8): P_t = 0.55*Fy*A_bar (only center bar contributes) Grout diameter equals drilled hole diameter in the uncased length Load reaching uncased length may be reduced by plunge length transfer (Section 5.15) No steel casing in the uncased bond zone Structural capacity of uncased length is typically less than cased length

figures.description: Geotechnical Capacity - Grout-to-Ground Bond Estimation of micropile geotechnical capacity based on grout-to-ground bond for preliminary and final design. Ultimate bond: R_bond = alpha_bond * pi * D_b * L_bond (Eq. 5-9) Allowable capacity: P_G-allowable = R_bond / FS; FS = 2.0 to 2.5 (Eq. 5-10) Table 5-3 provides alpha_bond values by soil/rock type and grouting Type (A, B, C, D) Type A in rock: 345-4150 kPa; Type B in sand: 70-360 kPa; Type B in clay: 25-190 kPa Higher bond values achieved with Type C and Type D grouting Presumptive values should be verified by site-specific load testing Bond zone diameter D_b may differ from casing diameter depending on grouting method

figures.description: Corrosion Protection Corrosion protection design for micropiles based on ground aggressiveness and loading conditions. Aggressive ground: pH < 4.5, resistivity < 2000 ohm-cm, sulfates > 200 ppm, chlorides > 100 ppm (Table 5-5) Table 5-6: corrosion protection recommendations by loading type and aggressiveness Casing compression in aggressive ground: minimum 1.6 mm section loss per AASHTO Core steel in tension/aggressive: epoxy coating, galvanization, or encapsulation required Minimum grout cover: 25 mm (1 in.) in soil, 12.5 mm (0.5 in.) in rock Corrosion protection must extend 5 m (15 ft) below corrosive material Double corrosion protection recommended for permanent tension micropiles in aggressive ground (Figure 5-17)

figures.caption: Detail of Load Transfer through the Casing Plunge Length
figures.description: Plunge Length and End Bearing Design of plunge length for load transfer and evaluation of end bearing for micropiles on rock. Plunge length: casing extension into bond zone to transfer load from cased to ground Transfer load (Eq. 5-25): P_transfer = (alpha_bond/FS) * pi * D_b * Plunge_Length Plunge length reduces load reaching the uncased bond zone Plunge length load transfer should be verified by load testing End bearing generally negligible for micropiles due to small cross-sectional area End bearing may be significant for micropiles on high-quality sound rock Nominal rock socket of 0.6 m (2 ft) used to verify competent rock bearing Structural capacity typically controls for end bearing micropiles on competent rock

figures.caption: Three-dimensional soil pile interaction
figures.description: Seismic Considerations Seismic design of micropile foundations including liquefaction, uplift, lateral loading, and battered pile considerations. Design for increased axial loads from overturning, lateral inertial loads, and liquefaction Three-dimensional soil-pile interaction: t-z (axial), p-y (lateral), torsional curves Vertical micropiles have limited lateral stiffness; battered piles preferred for lateral resistance AASHTO: FS = 1.0 for uplift from seismic forces Pile cap reinforcement ratio ~0.5% achieves fully ductile response (Trinh et al., 2004) Liquefaction reduces lateral resistance to 0.1-1.0% of non-liquefied value Battered micropiles reduce pore pressure buildup (FOREVER, 2003) Avoid battered micropiles where ground settlement is expected

ASTM D1143 (compression), D3689 (tension), D3966 (lateral) govern micropile testing Equipment: hydraulic jack, reaction beam, calibrated load cell, pressure gauge, dial gauges Compression reaction: adjacent piles, micropiles, ground anchors, or weighted platform Load cells required for verification/ultimate tests to maintain constant creep load; not required for proof tests Dial gauges on independent reference frame per ASTM Inclinometer in pile recommended for lateral tests: 10-20 pile diameters deep Strain gauge pairs can assess bending moments with depth

figures.caption: Load Displacement Curve of Verification Tests
figures.description: Micropile Load Testing Procedures Step-by-step load testing procedures for both verification and proof tests on micropile projects. Verification test: cyclic loading per Table 7-1 to 2.0-2.5x DL; record delta_t and delta_r Elastic movement: delta_e = delta_t - delta_r Proof test: monotonic loading per Table 7-2 to 160% DL Failure criterion: load-settlement slope > 0.15 mm/kN (0.025 in/kip) at 2x DL Davisson criterion not applicable to micropiles due to variable axial stiffness Creep acceptance: <= 1mm movement between 1-10 min at 1.3 DL hold Failed pile remedies: replacement piles, reduced capacity, modified installation, longer bond, or different type

figures.caption: Dynamic Test Set-Up for Micropile
figures.description: Other Load Testing Techniques Evaluating supplementary dynamic testing methods as alternatives or supplements to static micropile proof testing. PDA: requires pile hammer mobilization; CAPWAP data interpretation; cannot do creep, tension, or lateral Statnamic (Bermingham and James, 1989): gas-pressure impulse loading; cannot do creep or tension Both techniques may offer cost advantages for compression proof testing on large projects Neither technique can replace the creep test, which is currently the key acceptance criterion Data interpretation for both requires engineers with specialized knowledge of the methods Both methods not yet widely used for micropiles; experience still being developed

figures.caption: Cement Storage
figures.description: Inspection of Micropile Materials Receiving inspection for all micropile materials: cement, steel casing, reinforcing bars, and specialty corrosion-protection systems. Three compliance verification approaches: certification, visual inspection, or conformance testing All materials must be visually examined before installation Reinforcing steel: fiber rope lifting, mill certificates required, verify bar size Mill secondary pipe: no mill certificate available — requires tensile and chemical testing Light surface rust acceptable; deep flaky corrosion or pitting = rejection Epoxy-coated bars: padded bands and supports; repair epoxy damage per manufacturer Buy America: verify US manufacturing for applicable contracts

figures.caption: Reinforcement Centralizers
figures.description: Inspection of Construction Activities Field inspection of micropile drilling, reinforcement placement, and grouting operations. Loss of ground signs: casing sticking, excessive soil removal, surface subsidence Remove temporary casing while maintaining grout fill to prevent hole collapse Complete drilling, reinforcement, and grouting as continuous processes same day for weak/sensitive materials Maintain casing >= 0.3m above grade to prevent contamination of completed holes Centralizers at 2.5-3m intervals; verify centering of reinforcement Tremie grouting from bottom up; maintain positive grout head in tank Post-grouting pressures: typically 2-4 MPa; documented up to 6.5 MPa

figures.caption: Drill Rig Pressure Gauge
Grout Cubes for Compressive Strength Testing
figures.description: Required Project Documentation Documentation requirements for all micropile projects: load test records, installation logs, and grouting records. Production log (Table 8-1): record design vs. as-built for every pile — dimensions, drill method, soil descriptions, grout data Grouting records required daily: pressure and volume per pile Grout strength: 3 cubes (50mm) per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109; results after 48 hours Grout density: Baroid Mud Balance per API RP 13B-1; perform at least once per pile Target grout SG = 1.8-1.9 corresponds to w/c ≈ 0.45 Density test preferred as immediate quality check vs. strength test (48-hour lag)
